etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
paragraphs: From Middle English galle, from Old English ġealla, galla, from Proto-West Germanic *gallā, from Proto-Germanic *gallǭ.

The figurative senses (e.g., impudence, brazenness, chutzpah) are related to the literal sense (i.e., bile) via the lasting linguocultural effects of humorism, which governed Western medicine for many centuries before the advent of scientific medicine.
Related to Dutch gal, German Galle, Swedish galle, galla, Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ). Also remotely related with yellow and gold.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
paragraphs: From Middle English galle, from Old English gealla (“a fretted spot on the skin”), from Proto-West Germanic *gallō, from Proto-Germanic *gallô (“infirmity, swelling, lesion”).
senses: (countable) A sore on a horse caused by an ill-fitted or ill-adjusted saddle; a saddle sore.
(pathology, countable) A sore or open wound caused by chafing, which may become infected, as with a blister.
(ergative) To chafe, to rub or subject to friction; to create a sore on the skin.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
paragraphs: From Middle English galle, from Old French galle, from Latin galla (“oak-apple”).
senses: (phytopathology) A blister or tumor-like growth found on the surface of plants, caused by various pathogens, especially the burrowing of insect larvae into the living tissues, such as that of the common oak gall wasp (Cynips quercusfolii).
A bump-like imperfection resembling a gall.
(transitive) To impregnate with a decoction of gallnuts in dyeing.
